segments.text: Start with one hundred thousand ASCII code points in a compact CPython string. Their internal character slots use one byte each.
Concatenate U plus one F six hundred. The new result needs four-byte slots for every code point, including the unchanged ASCII prefix. The original string is not modified.

A supplied CPython three point eleven point fifteen observation reports one hundred thousand forty-nine bytes before, and four hundred thousand eighty bytes after. Those totals include object overhead; this is not a new measurement.
UTF-eight is different. Its ASCII prefix still uses one byte per code point, and the added code point contributes four bytes. The encoded payload grows by four, not fourfold.
Not every non-ASCII character forces four-byte slots. U plus zero zero E nine stays in the one-byte class, while U plus four E two D uses two. Code-point range is the key, not an emoji label.
